what_it_does: XGBoost is a popular machine-learning algorithm that makes predictions by running an input through a collection of decision trees — branching if-then rules that ultimately output a score. When XGBoost is accelerated on an FPGA (a reconfigurable chip that can be wired to run specific computations very fast), the chip's power consumption changes slightly depending on which branches of the tree are taken for a given input. An attacker who can measure that power consumption over many predictions can statistically reverse-engineer the tree structure — a technique called a power side-channel attack — effectively stealing the model. This paper demonstrates that attack in practice on a hardware platform called Sakura-X running an FPGA accelerator called FAXID, showing that an adversary can deduce the decision thresholds and features the model uses. The result is a concrete warning that hardware implementations of tree-based models need power-side-channel countermeasures, even though such attacks are better known in the cryptography world. Details of the full attack methodology and how much of the model can be recovered are in the full paper.
